Skullgirls is genuinely a great game. The music is an absolute jam, gameplay is enjoyable, the humor is lovely, characters are fun in every way, and the art is beautiful. This is one of the biggest vibes I've had the pleasure of experiencing in a fighting game. If you like jazz, 2d fighting games, and don't shudder at the sight of a woman, give Skullgirls a try. The only reason I leave a negative review is because of censorship, followed by a lack of foreseeable support.

After the original dev team broke apart due to horrendous management following the attempted removal of the lead designer, Hidden Variable Studios & Future Club were to take control of Skullgirls and keep it afloat. These new devs added additional paid characters to play as, but proceeded to censor content that has been in the game since a decade before.

Various references to and depictions of sexual content, race, and fascism were removed in 2015 (following the rebranding of Skullgirls as 2nd Encore) & 2023.
In 2015, some animations were changed to obstruct visible panties, and Lab Zero Games promised no more censorship afterwards.
In 2020, ownership changed. In 2023, the game was censored as a whole.
Some of these changes took form in sprite & art alterations: changing the colors of undergarments, removing a comb from an Italian character's head because her burst animation turned her hair into an afro (this was in the name of removing racial stereotypes, but her brown clone still has the comb for some reason), replacing Valentine's cross imagery with shurikens (blame the actual Red Cross organization for this, since they copyrighted the medical symbol we all grew up with) ,and removing Nazi symbolism from the Black Egrets (the villains). Much of the art from the downloadable artbook was removed in line with updates made to the game itself.
In terms of actual content, multiple voice lines, voice packs, & lines were removed; some were sex jokes while others were references to other games, the story, or the community (two examples are the "Barely Legal" 18-hit combo rating, and Big Band's "Cheen" line from his voice pack). Story panels related to the police brutality & sexual assault suffered by Big Band & Filia, respectively, were removed entirely. Gallery art was altered in the same way as all the other changes.

The only way to experience the game with its original story and art is to download a pre-censorship patch and replace your game files. Or you can got to Properties -> Game Versions & Betas -> entercode 'ireallyfearchange' and select that build from 2016.

Development for this game has also ceased in the wake of legal disputes between the devs & publisher, forgoing future content additions and leaving the censorship as is, unless the development team(s) shift again. Online play still works, though, so its worth buying if you want to play with a friend on another computer.

What really crossed the line for me was seeing content that had been promised and in some cases already delivered later walked back and removed. Taking something away from players after the fact and then dismissing their concerns is just not okay in my book. At its core, the game is still fun. It looks great, has a ton of content, and a surprisingly broad story for a fighting game. If you enjoy the gameplay loop, you could easily sink countless hours into it. None of that is the problem. The issue started after the original creators were pushed out and a new team took over. From that point on, it felt like the game’s identity began to change. Long standing elements were suddenly reinterpreted as inappropriate, with content altered or removed in ways that actively made things worse rather than more tasteful. This is especially frustrating because the game was designed with that tone and style from the very beginning it wasn’t added later, it was the game. What makes it harder to swallow is the inconsistency. Certain things are censored or changed in game, while similar or more explicit material is openly endorsed elsewhere. It comes across as performative rather than principled, and it leaves the impression that decisions are being made to appease social pressure instead of respecting the original vision or the existing fanbase. You can support inclusivity without rewriting history or talking down to your own players. Trying to please everyone while ignoring the people who were already there just ends up alienating both sides. I still think the game itself is strong, but the way it’s been handled post handover leaves a bad taste. The controversy didn’t have to happen it was entirely avoidable.

Skullgirls is a 2D arcade action fighting game released on the PC in August 2013. The game was originally released on the consoles in 2012 and had great success. 

Skullgirls differs from the fighting games that we have lately, in that you can actually fight in teams of two or three, as well as the single sided matches.  All of the rules are the same as usual, however in team matches, the team which has the most health when adding them all together wins in the event of the time running out.  Each of the characters have a wide array of move sets to learn, and combos. Some of the special attacks are just amazing to watch. The animations on all of the characters is absolutely flawless. 

Since Skullgirls focuses a lot on the team matches, that means you are going to get plenty of double teams and dirty tricks being played by "non active" characters, and even hyper combos. 

All of the environments that you fight in are absolutely stunning as well. Even though they are pre-rendered, they are presented in a stunning art style which fits right in with the game. I would of liked to have seen maybe a little environment interactivity, but I guess you can't ask for everything. 

The story mode in Skullgirls isn't all that brilliant. It is extremely short, and you can blast through the story mode on any character in under 20 minutes if you try.  Yes you get the story and plot out of it, but all of the battles are the same each time you play and there is no varying. This is easily the shortest fighting game story mode I have played. 

Sound effects and sound track really are done well in Skullgirls. They are certainly way above par in the fighting genre.  You can actually. The sound track is amazing - you can purchase it separately here https://skullgirls.com/media/music/ if you are into that kind of thing as well. 

Skullgirls has varying levels of difficulty in the regular, normal, easy and hard modes. Certainly steer clear from easy mode as it offers no challenge at all. I really couldn't keep up hard mode even on the story mode. There is also a couple of other modes to play in too - the normal arcade mode and versus mode. This game also has a very good tutorial which introduces all of the elements and some of the combos for your characters. 

Like I said, you can finish the story mode on a single player mode in under twenty minutes. Of course you can replay it with all of the characters which is about seven or eight (not including the DLC), which is in my opinion a bit low. Where you are going to get your mileage out of Skullgirls is in the arcade mode and in the multiplayer mode.  I have spent about 6 hours playing online (mostly getting my self owned over and over again), and I am having a blast playing. This is easily the best multiplayer fighter I've played in a while. 

I really strongly recommend Skullgirls, just off the pure fact that it is highly addictive to play, and you can pick up and play so easily. The inclusion of a well put together tutorial and combo system makes this game head and shoulders above most other fighting games of this type.

Skullgirls is a well made game, and I appreciate the Linux support, which is all to rare in fighting games.  The art and aesthetic are quite nice, and the music is unique.

However, the recent changes that have been made to the game, most notably removing content that players have paid for, is disappointing to say the least.  This game has had the content in question for nearly a decade, and yet now is the time to go back and remove it?  It's not like the changes will draw new customers, just alienate old ones.  And that's the sad truth.  It's not being done for the benefit of players, but for pushing an agenda that was never a part of the game in the first place.

This goes on to be an even larger philosophical issue when it comes to purchasing a game and owning it.  In the old days, when you bought a game it was complete, and devs couldn't change it without issuing a new release. Now games can be updated at a whim, and so the players put the trust on the developer that they will maintain the game that the player purchased.  Sure there may be balance updates, but those are generally welcome, as they are done through community guidance.  There may be new content, which is fine because it keeps the community engaged.  But removing content is a betrayal of that trust the players put in the developer.

As such, I won't be buying any future games from this developer, as I've lost trust in them as a customer.  (If they ever put out a new game.  It seems like the talent that's been creating the games has moved on to other projects...)

A game thats clearly a passion project by developers deeply ingrained in the genre; probably one of the best balanced, from beginner to pro, 2d fighters to ever come about.

-Pros-

-Every character is viable and yes literally every character is viable so long as their role is utilized properly
-As a result of all characters being viable the only real 'tier' list comes down to a matter of match ups in team composition in tag matches
-Combo system is intuitive, anti-infinite, and simple with a light->medium->heavy linking system
-Frame buffers and combo mechanics make for no frustrating 1 frame links or split second muscle memory shenanigans
-Training and challenges have to be some of the highest quality to ever grace a fighting game; they'll teach you combos, mechanics, mechanics of the mechanics, and how its interacting with the game itself through hit, stun, and frame data
-Difficulty is subjective but the AI is pretty well balanced so long as you're willing to put in the work
-Story mode is wonderfully done and has fantastic artwork
-The game itself is a beautiful example of hand drawn artwork
-Literally EVERY character and frame is hand drawn; it makes everything exceedingly smooth and crisp
-This also applies to hitboxes: Skullgirls has an obscene amount of detail to its hitboxes
-Online is still alive and while you're liable to be stomped at this point in time it's fantastic to jump in for a match or 3

-Cons-

-Learning curve is substantial and while the trials do help nothing prepares you for getting stomped an hour straight in multiplayer
-Sadly reached the end of its support after 5 years; not a con per se but a shame to see such a wonderful game finally taper off
-Multiplayer is also tapering off at this point and with all the new fighters pushing it from the spotlight it can be hard to find a match without finding a group or friend

Lab Zero has made a great game, a great fighting game, and helped further the genre with this spiffy little gem.

Set in the Canopy Kingdom, Skullgirls tells the tale of eight female warriors as they fight to reclaim a wish-granting artifact known as the "Skull Heart" from the monstrous Skullgirl. As legend has it, every seven years this enigmatic Skull Heart grants a wish to a young woman... but this power can come at a terrible price. If her heart is impure, her wish will be twisted and she herself will be transformed into a Skullgirl.

Developed by newcomer Reverge Labs, Skullgirls is a fast-paced 2D fighting game. Starring a cast of feisty female warriors, Skullgirls is a multi-layered fighter featuring all-new game systems for veteran fighting game fans while also making the intimidating genre enjoyable and accessible to the casual gamer.

This game is fast, polished, and has tons of quality-of-life features that other fighting games lack. On a surface level it is very easy and fun to sit down and play. However as somebody who is interested in practicing and learning FGs, it feels a bit daunting, especially after watching high-level play. But it might not be for the reasons you'd expect.

Execution is pretty easy in this game due to a lenient buffer system. Combos aren't that hard either, mainly consisting of button strings with jump cancels, ending in specials then supers. Yes, there is a lot of complexity when you add character swapping and assists to the mix, but that's par for the course in versus games. 

What feels intimidating about this game is how it is less reliant on traditional knockdown/oki play. Knockdowns and advantage states absolutely still exist, but it is much harder to keep people on the defensive due to how powerful pushblock is. You can absolutely lock people down with assists, but without them advantage states never last very long. So, the way you maintain your advantage is never letting people escape your combos. How do you do this? With mid-combo resets. Endless, brain-twisting resets.

The thing about combos in this game is that while they are easy to input, timing matters a lot because hitstun is pretty low when compared to most FGs. Typically I drop combos because I press the wrong buttons/mis-input a move. In this game, its usually because I'm going slightly too fast or slightly too slow. You can weaponize this timing variability to 'drop' a combo on purpose, letting your opponent leave hitstun so that you can then mix them up and start a new combo. Watching high level play, this happens CONSTANTLY. Its an aspect that makes this game unique, and it also means that blocking against a player that knows what they're doing can sometimes feel impossible. You have to be on your toes watching for left/right-high/low-strike/throw mixups WHILE you're being combo'd. It's nuts.

Now, at a low level, this doesnt really apply; it takes a lot of practice to pull off resets like this. Getting to the point where you have enough control over your character to drop your combos on purpose to mix your opponent takes a long time. THIS is what makes the game intimidating to me- the combined level of execution and character knowledge to pull off resets and know when they're coming is some real nth-level massive brain shit. Its dope to watch, but I don't know if I will realistically be able to get there.

So yeah, this game is really cool, and is pretty easy to get into and play on a simple level. But to really know and take advantage of the system? I feel like that'll take years. I don't know if thats true, but watching high level play is daunting. I love being able to watch the pros and go "I wanna learn how to do that." I can't really do that with this game, at least not for another couple hundred hours.

This game comes with multiple measures to punish longer combos, which inevitably encourage the intentional dropping of the combo.
The simplest form is high/low, which seems to be not so bad.
Of course you can add the grab with the cost of heavier damage fall off, 33/33/33 seems still manageable.
And there's also cross ups to all of this, it's A LITERAL DICE at this point.
Did I forget to mention that some characters can do this airborne(albeit without low so a bit fewer options)?

The worst part is that not all characters have a tool to properly punish every reset, which I think nullifies the whole defense of the resets.
If the opponent cannot punish high, you can just do high cross ups.
If the opponent cannot punish you airborne, do whatever you want, but in the air.
It's like RPS but the your fingers are glued together.

This game is more fun to watch than it is to play. I respect the creators. This has some amazing animation and not a bad story, but at the end of the day, it's a fighting game that's unapproachable by anyone that hasn't played fighting games their whole life. And I've played the tutorials. I've tried my best to learn this game, but the mere fact that it takes so much effort to learn the BASICS of this game, is extremely telling to how bad this game is at welcoming new players.

If you like fighting games, the chances are you either already own this game, or you've heard and seen so much about it already to make up your mind. Compared to other games of the same caliber, this is pretty cheap and therefore a great deal so by all means, buy this game, HOWEVER if you have never learned a fighting game beyond button mashing and maybe knowing how to do a shoryuken, this game is not for you.

You can look up art or watch videos if you just like the visuals, unless you just really like the creators themselves and want to support their hard work. I've personally spent hours trying to learn this game and I still feel like a beginner. And the in-game tutorial doesn't help much. As soon as you get the inputs they display for you it's on to the next lesson. They don't give it time to sink in. You have to repeat the lessons yourself, then go into the training mode and keep practicing. It's that nearly impossible learning curve, a need for specific controllers, and natural abilities some people simply don't have the luxury of being born with that make fighting games feel less like a "game" and more like a sport.

I don't personally have much experience with fighthing games, so I can't suggest a perfect alternative. If you still want a "fighting" game but not a fighting game, I'd suggest Rivals of Aether or Slap City if you want a fighting game that's still fun and not impossible to get into. I'd say Super Smash Bros, but it seems odd to recommend a game on another platform worth 6 times as much not including DLC. And Rivals of Aether has mods! There are hours of fun just trying new characters fans of the game made, and you don't need to play through a tutorial to understand the most basic fundamentals of the game. And Slap City if even closer to Smash Bros than Aether is. It has multiple game modes and characters with unique movesets that aren't direct copies of other characters. You can tell a lot of love went into everything in the game.

Unless you are already someone that loves 2d fighting games, don't buy this game. Just watch it. Fighting games are still fun spectator sports without ever picking up the games
